items.title: Hitler nearly walked out of the Nazi Party in 1921
items.claim: In July 1921, Hitler threatened to resign from the NSDAP unless he was given dictatorial control. What happened?

options.text: He was expelled and founded a rival party
The committee accepted his terms by a vote of 543 to 1 — the lone dissenter being a printer named Posch
He was forced to share leadership with Anton Drexler
The party split in two, with Hitler taking the Munich faction

items.reveal:
Anton Drexler had founded the German Workers' Party in 1919. Hitler joined in September 1919 as member 555 (the numbering started at 500 to inflate membership). By 1921 he was the party's most effective speaker.

When Drexler tried to merge with another nationalist group, Hitler resigned in protest, then demanded the chairmanship with dictatorial powers as the price of returning. The 29 July 1921 vote went 543 to 1.
items.why: Hitler's rise feels inevitable in hindsight. In 1921 he was a fringe agitator in a fringe party negotiating his way to control of an organisation with no national presence. Contingency, again.

items.title: The Glorious Revolution was a Dutch invasion
items.claim: William of Orange landed in Devon on 5 November 1688. How large was the force?

options.text: A diplomatic mission of a few hundred men
Around 15,000 troops on 463 ships — larger than the Spanish Armada
Only James II's English defectors, no foreign troops
A small English army recruited in advance by Parliament

items.reveal:
Seven English nobles (the 'Immortal Seven') invited William in June 1688. He landed at Brixham, Devon, with 15,000-21,000 Dutch troops, plus thousands of horses and 50 cannon. James II's army melted; key officers (including John Churchill, the future Duke of Marlborough) defected.

James fled to France in December. The Convention Parliament (January 1689) declared the throne vacant and offered it to William and Mary. The Bill of Rights followed in December 1689.

The Williamite War in Ireland (Boyne 1690) and the Highland war in Scotland (Killiecrankie 1689) were anything but bloodless.
items.why: The 'Glorious Revolution' as bloodless English self-determination is a Whig myth. It was a foreign-backed coup with extensive bloodshed in Ireland and Scotland — successful, but not peaceful.

items.title: Children under 10 worked underground in British coal mines until 1842
items.claim: What did the Mines Act of 1842 prohibit?

options.text: All child labour in the UK
Underground employment for women and girls, and for boys under 10 — following Lord Ashley's (later Shaftesbury) commission report with illustrations of children pulling coal trucks
Coal mining itself, switching the country to oil

items.reveal:
The 1842 Royal Commission report on children in mines included engravings of half-naked children — boys as young as 5 acting as 'trappers' opening ventilation doors, girls and women hauling coal in chains. The illustrations shocked Parliament.

The Act banned women and girls underground entirely and boys under 10. Earlier factory legislation (1819, 1833, 1844) limited child working hours and required schooling. Robert Owen's New Lanark mills (from 1800) had already shown a different model.
items.why: 'Reform' was driven partly by humanitarian shock and partly by middle-class anxiety about working-class women. The Acts solved one problem (underground child labour) without addressing others (above-ground work continued for decades).
